title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary:
This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure configuration, model-serving requirements, observability expectations, performance targets, and ADR (Architectural Decision Record) process. It is intended as the one-stop reference for cross-functional teams (runtime, infra, platform, SDKs, SRE, and product) when designing or changing services that impact production inference, latency, cost, or reliability.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all services that implement or operate on the Redwood public API, internal RPCs between serving components, infra provisioning for Dedicated/Private deployments, and any customer-facing dashboards (Console).
- Excludes small experimental sandbox projects under /experimental with explicit TTL and owner approval.

1) API standards
Purpose: ensure stable, discoverable, and backwards-compatible APIs for customers and internal clients.
Required conventions:
- Versioning: semantic version in the path for major breaking changes (e.g., /v1/generate). Minor and patch-level changes must follow compatibility rules and use feature flags for rollout.
- Idempotency: write-like operations must accept Idempotency-Key header.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for list endpoints (cursor, page_size). Avoid offset for large result sets.
- Error model: All endpoints must return a JSON error envelope: {"error": {"code": "<short_code>", "message": "Human readable", "details": []}}. Use HTTP status codes per RFC 7231.
- Schema: public API schemas are canonical and must be documented in OpenAPI (YAML) under api-examples/openapi/. Example response schema for text generation: 
{
  "request_id": "uuid",
  "model": "redwood-v2-small",
  "output": [{"text": "...", "tokens": 42}],
  "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 43, "completion_tokens": 42}
}
- Backwards compatibility policy: additive changes (new fields) allowed; removing or renaming fields requires major version bump. Behavioral changes (e.g., tokenization) must be gated with a rollout plan and documented in release notes.
- Rate limiting and quotas: standard response headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset and 429 responses with Retry-After.
Ownership: API guild + eng-developer-experience.

2) Coding standards
Purpose: maintain readable, secure, and testable code across repos. These standards are enforced via linters, CI checks, and mandatory code review.
Language-specific highlights:
- Python (services and SDKs): PEP8, type hints for public functions, mypy strictness level: error for missing return type on public APIs. Async code must use asyncio and avoid blocking calls on the event loop (run_in_executor allowed with justification).
- Go (infrastructure services): gofmt must pass; errors must be wrapped with contextual messages; context.Context must be first arg for functions that perform IO.
- Rust/C++ (runtime hotpaths): prefer explicit ownership and avoid runtime allocation in hot loops; use fuzzing for memory safety validation.
General rules:
- Maximum PR size: 400 lines of change without manager approval.
- Tests: unit tests for all public functions; integration tests for cross-service contracts; golden file tests for model outputs used in regressions.
- Security: use static analysis (Snyk/OSS-fix), no hard-coded secrets. Secrets must be read from KMS-integrated secret store.
- Formatting and pre-commit: pre-commit hooks required for all repos. CI gates: lint, unit tests, type checks, and a lightweight security scan.
Ownership: eng-developer-experience.

3) Infrastructure standards
Goal: consistent, secure, and repeatable infra for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
Provisioning:
- Use Terraform for cloud resources. Module registry lives in eng-infra/terraform-and-iac. Avoid ad-hoc cloud console changes.
- Resource tags: all production resources must include tags: {owner, team, environment, cost-center}.
- Network: default to least-privilege security groups; only designated ingress for model-serving (TLS 1.2+).
Compute standards for serving:
| Service class | CPU | Memory | GPU (if required) | Typical use case |
|---------------|-----|--------|-------------------|------------------|
| control-plane  | 2 vCPU | 8 GB  | n/a               | API gateways, routers |
| standard-worker| 8 vCPU | 32 GB | T4/A10 or equivalent | embedding workers, small model inference |
| gpu-inference  | 16 vCPU| 128 GB| H100 / A100 80GB or H-series | large model low-latency serving |
Deployment and rollout:
- All infra changes must be made via Terraform and code-reviewed. Nightly infra plan runs for drift detection.
- Blue/green or canary network-level rollouts for capacity changes that affect latency.
Cost control:
- Autoscaling policies must include upper limit and preemptible spot pools where supported for non-SLA traffic.
Ownership: eng-infra.

4) Model-serving standards
Purpose: ensure safe, predictable, and efficient serving of models across hosted and private modes.
Requirements:
- Model packaging: models must include manifest.yaml with fields: name, version, architecture, quantization_profile, kv_cache_supported (true/false), max_context_tokens, recommended_batch_size, memory_estimate_gb.
- Serving contract: Any model listed in the catalog must implement the same inference contract (predict API) with deterministic metadata response (model_id, version, tokenizer, float_precision).
- Quantization: quantization profiles must be attached to model artifacts and validated against QA prompts. A/B quantization rollouts require a regression test against baseline prompt set with thresholds (see Performance section).
- Caching & batching: default runtime batching must be enabled for throughput classes; but latency-sensitive routes must be able to disable batching per-policy. KV cache eviction policies documented per model.
- Safety checks: model outputs must pass a lightweight safety filter pre-deploy; higher-risk models require human-in-the-loop evaluation.
SLOs for model-serving endpoints (baseline hosted offering):
- Availability: 99.95% monthly uptime.
- Latency targets: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 180ms, p99 < 500ms for small-medium models on dedicated pools. For large models (context > 8k) p95 target is < 1.5s when served on H100 class nodes.
Ownership: eng-serving-runtime + applied-ml-and-evals for onboarding tests.

5) Observability standards
Goal: actionable telemetry for incident response, capacity planning, and performance tuning.
Minimal signal requirements per service:
- Metrics (Prometheus): request_rate, request_errors, latency_histogram (p50/p95/p99), token_rate, gpu_utilization, memory_pressure. All metrics must be tagged by service, model, region, and customer_tier (where applicable).
- Tracing: distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) with 200ms sampling for high-volume routes, 100% sampling for error traces. Traces must include request_id and model_version.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields timestamp, level, service, host, request_id, msg, extra. Do not log PII or secrets.
- Dashboards: each service must have a standard dashboard (latency, errors, throughput, cost-per-token) and an on-call checklist. Templates live in eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts.
- Alerts: SLO-based alerting (see SRE policy). MTTI objective: < 5 minutes for Sev1. Pager thresholds: error rate > 1% over 5 minutes or p95 latency > target + 50% triggers P1.
Ownership: eng-platform + eng-sre.

6) Performance standards and benchmarking
Objective: predictable inference unit economics and latency.
Benchmarks and metrics:
- Benchmark harness: use benchmarking-and-perf-suite with synthetic and real prompt sets (prompt-sets-and-benchmarks). All model onboarding must include: cold-start latency, steady-state throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost-per-1M-tokens estimate for reference hardware.
- Regression thresholds: when a new runtime or kernel change increases p95 latency by > 10% or cost-per-token by > 5% for a tracked workload, the change must be blocked and investigated.
- Load testing: monthly organized game-day tests for capacity boundaries; results recorded in eng-platform/retrospectives.
Perf optimizations guidance:
- Use continuous batching and prefix caching for stable workloads.
- Kernel selection: prefer fused attention kernels for sequence lengths < 2k; otherwise use memory-optimized kernels.
Ownership: eng-serving-runtime + applied-ml-and-evals.

7) ADR process (Architectural Decision Records)
Purpose: provide a discoverable history of major architectural decisions and trade-offs.
How to write an ADR:
1. Create a short title and date (YYYY-MM-DD).
2. State the decision in a short summary.
3. Document context and alternatives considered.
4. State consequences and migration plan.
5. Assign owner and reviewers.
6. File ADR under architecture-and-standards/decision-records with numeric ID.
Example ADR (abbreviated):
- ADR-2026-01: Unified Model Router (adopted)
  - Summary: Route inference requests to model variants by policy (latency, cost, region).
  - Context: Multiple services had bespoke routing causing inconsistent fallbacks and capacity pressure.
  - Alternatives: maintain per-service routing (rejected), central router (adopted).
  - Decision: build central model-router service with a policy engine and health-aware routing.
  - Consequences: additional operational surface area; simplifies client logic and enables cross-service fallback.
  - Owner: Marcus Chen.

8) Rollout and change management
Standard rollout steps for infra or API-impacting changes:
1. Draft proposal and ADR if architectural.
2. Add feature flag and default to safe behavior.
3. Unit + integration + canary tests.
4. Canary rollout (2% traffic for 2 hours) with automated SLO checks.
5. Incremental roll to 25% for 24 hours, then 50% for 24 hours, then 100%.
6. Post-rollout verification and runbook signoff.
Emergency rollback: document a single-step rollback in runbooks/runbooks for the service; aim for < 15 minutes rollback time for P1 incidents.

9) Ownership matrix and contacts
- API standards: eng-developer-experience (owner) — contact: eng-dx@redwood-inference.com
- Infra standards: eng-infra (owner) — contact: infra@redwood-inference.com
- Model-serving standards: eng-serving-runtime + applied-ml-and-evals (owners) — contact: runtime-team@redwood-inference.com
- Observability: eng-platform + eng-sre (owners) — contact: observability@redwood-inference.com

Appendix A — Quick reference SLOs and thresholds:
- Platform availability (control plane): 99.99% monthly.
- Model-serving availability: 99.95% monthly.
- Latency thresholds (hosted small-medium): p50 < 60ms, p95 < 180ms, p99 < 500ms.
- Error budget burn alert: > 2% of monthly budget consumed triggers risk review.

Appendix B — Example Terraform tagging policy snippet:
resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  tags = {
    Owner = var.owner
    Team = var.team
    Environment = var.environment
    CostCenter = var.cost_center
  }
}

Appendix C — Example ADR template (text):
Title: ADR-YYYY-NN: Short title
Status: proposed | accepted | superseded
Context: ...
Decision: ...
Consequences: ...
Owner: Name, team
Related: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records
